chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Zurarah who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who was killed, and he had a brother in Dar al-Hijrah (the city of emigration) and another brother in Dar al-Badw (the desert/bedouin dwellings) who had not emigrated. I asked: Do you think if the emigrant forgives and the bedouin wants to kill, does he have that right? He said: 'The bedouin does not have the right to kill an emigrant until he emigrates. If the emigrant forgives, then his forgiveness is valid.' I said to him: And what about the bedouin's share of the inheritance? He said: 'As for the inheritance, it is for him, and he has his portion from the blood-money of his killed brother, if the blood-money is taken.'

key_terms.دَارُ اَلْبَدْوِ: Dar al-Badw (the desert or bedouin dwellings)
key_terms.دَارُ اَلْهِجْرَةِ: Dar al-Hijrah (the city of emigration, typically Kufa or Medina)

ai.seo_question: What are the inheritance rights of a brother who did not emigrate when his brother did?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Baqir clarifies the legal status of the 'non-emigrating' brother (al-Badawi) versus the 'emigrating' brother (al-Muhajir) regarding inheritance and blood-money (diya). The ruling establishes that the non-emigrating brother retains his full share of inheritance and diya, and crucially, the emigrating brother’s forgiveness of the killer is legally valid even on behalf of the non-emigrating brother, highlighting the flexibility in kinship rights within early Islamic jurisprudence.
